title: Removing the defender: does it really win?
outcomes: Finds the capture of a defender that wins material when the theme is not named
Recounts the target square after the removal before playing it
Spots the second guard (a pawn, for example) that makes the removal win nothing
Recognises a position where taking the defender only trades pieces

steps.text:
In *Removing the defender* you found the capture that takes a sole defender. This lesson is about deciding whether to play it. Two questions before you capture the defender:
**Does another piece take over its job?**
**After the whole exchange, am I ahead?**
A capture that only trades pieces wins nothing.

steps.caption: White to move. The knight on e7 is guarded by the queen on d8.

line.say: The queen takes the guard of the knight on e7.
The knight lost its guard, so the rook takes it.

claims.statement: The engine's best move is Qxd8 (depth 16).
Along the engine's best-defence line Qxd8 nets White at least a minor piece.

steps.text:
**When it works:** the defender is the only guard of the target, and after every recapture you have won more than you gave up. Use the counting values 1, 3, 3, 5, 9 (a rule of thumb, not true worth) to add it up.
**When it fails:** another piece guards the target after the removal, or the exchange is an even trade. Recount the square, including every recapture.

steps.title: Same removal, one more guard
steps.prompt: Predict first: in the second position a black pawn stands on h7 instead of h6.
Before you captured a defender, did you recount the target square after the whole exchange, or only check that the defender could be taken?
